newsitem.title: USA: CME butter futures return after 20-year absence.
newsitem.headline: CME butter futures return after 20-year absence.

text.p: After a 20-year absence, butter futures trading returned Thursday to the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.

About 25 traders crowded into the small trading area on the exchange's livestock floor. The first contract traded at 109.93 cents a lb for February 1997 delivery, but later slipped to trade at 106.85. The April 1997 contract first traded at 110.00 cents, then slipped to 108.00.

Developers of the contract expressed optimism for its success because of small U.S. stockpiles against increased domestic consumption. After two hours of trading, some 112 February contracts and 25 April contracts had changed hands.
"Milk production is off across the U.S.," said Jerry Klose, operations manager for butter processing for Land O'Lakes, Inc.
Klose said high feed prices in the past year had caused dairymen to reduce herd sizes and cut milk production.
After helping ring the bell to start trading, Klose said domestic demand for butter had risen steadily in recent years, driving prices higher. However, he expects high prices will stabilize usage.
"We think we've reached a plateau, because demand will diminish somewhat because of the price," he said.
Robert Prosi, chairman of the CME's dairy products committee, said in a statement that cash butter prices this year have ranged from 70 cents a lb to $1.50.
CME Chairman Jack Sandner said trading of the CME's previous butter contract ended in 1976 because of U.S. government-established price supports.
Now, with government supplies low, price supports are no longer a market factor.
Beginning Friday, CME butter futures will trade daily from 0800 CDT/1300 GMT to 1310 CDT/1810 GMT.
